topics.title: Pattern overview
topics.summary: Make an already useful object usable through the interface a caller already requires. Worked example: A gram-based parcel rule. Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.

blocks.title: Learning objectives
items: Translate an existing device API into an application contract.
Explain borrowing and conversion boundaries.
Test units, invalid readings, and rounding behavior.

blocks.text: The client calls the target operation. An adapter satisfies that target contract, calls the existing service through its different interface, and translates the result. In the normal attached C++ variant, Adapter inherits Target and stores an Adaptee pointer. In the multiple-inheritance variant, Adapter inherits both Target and Adaptee; Request calls the inherited SpecificRequest. That second adapter has its own Adaptee base subobject. It does not wrap the separate adaptee allocated by main.

cards.question: What problem does Adapter address?
cards.answer: Make an already useful object usable through the interface a caller already requires. Worked example: A gram-based parcel rule. Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.

cards.question: What is Adapter?
cards.answer: A boundary object that translates an existing service into a contract another caller needs.

cards.question: What is Adaptee?
cards.answer: The existing service whose interface or meaning must be translated.

cards.question: What is Class adapter?
cards.answer: An adapter implemented by inheriting from a target interface and a legacy class.

cards.question: What is Unit contract?
cards.answer: The agreement about what physical unit a number represents.

cards.question: Why is merely renaming milligrams to grams an incorrect Adapter?
cards.answer: It leaves units and error meanings wrong. The target contract requires conversion and rejection, not only a matching method name.

cards.question: Does the attached multiple-inheritance Adapter adapt the Adaptee object separately allocated in main?
cards.answer: No. Its inherited SpecificRequest operates on its own Adaptee base subobject. The separate object is used only for the direct demonstration.

cards.question: Why is a reference member not proof that the scale owns its device?
cards.answer: A reference is a borrow. The LegacyScale must outlive ScaleAdapter; destroying the device first leaves the adapter with an invalid reference.

cards.question: Would renaming milligrams to grams be a correct adapter?
cards.answer: No. The units differ by a factor of one thousand. Interface compatibility includes meaning and error behavior, not only method names.

cards.question: Why subtract calibration after conversion in this example?
cards.answer: The offset is measured in grams. Subtracting it from raw milligrams would mix units and produce a numerically plausible but wrong result.

cards.question: When can the adapter be a free function instead of a class?
cards.answer: When the caller needs one conversion and no persistent Scale interface or borrowed device. A class is useful when existing client code already consumes Scale polymorphically.

cards.question: What additional test is needed if floating readings replace integer milligrams?
cards.answer: Test nonfinite values and rounding near boundaries. The current integer device cannot produce NaN, but a new floating device can.

cards.question: Does a valid converted value prove the device reading was valid?
cards.answer: No. A negative device error might become plausible after careless arithmetic. Validate the raw error signal before converting or calibrating.

cards.question: Why keep light_enough independent of LegacyScale?
cards.answer: Its rule is about grams and a Scale contract. Keeping the old device API outside the client makes replacement devices easier to integrate and test.

topics.title: The problem: one program, two meanings of weight
topics.summary: A parcel station decides whether a sample weighs at most two grams. Its application already asks a Scale for grams. A replacement device is not available. The old device returns an integer count of milligrams through milligrams(), and a negative value means the device failed. We must reuse that device without teaching every parcel rule its old spelling, units, and error convention. The answer must preserve fractions: 1,250 milligrams means 1.25 grams.

blocks.text: For one caller, the simplest reasonable answer is a direct conversion. Read the integer, reject negative results, and divide by 1000.0. A helper function could keep that operation in one place. If every caller can use that helper, stop there. A class does not improve a problem that is already solved clearly. Our added constraint is different: existing rules accept a Scale reference and may receive several kinds of scales at run time.

discussion.answer: It compares different units and rejects a parcel that actually weighs 1.25 grams. Renaming a method is insufficient; the boundary must translate both the number and the device's error convention.

topics.title: The failure that calls for a translator
topics.summary: Passing LegacyScale straight to light_enough does not compile. It is not a Scale, and it has no grams member. Merely renaming milligrams would still leave the wrong unit and would treat a failure signal as a very light parcel. Changing every rule would mix device concerns with parcel rules. Each new device would repeat that work.

blocks.text: An adapter is an object that makes an existing service meet another interface. An interface is the set of operations and promises callers may use. ScaleAdapter meets Scale by implementing grams. Inside that method it calls the old device, checks its result, and translates the unit. The caller sees grams throughout. The old device does not know that an adapter exists. This is useful at a boundary where two independently developed pieces already disagree.

topics.title: What the C++ mechanism does
topics.summary: The colon in class ScaleAdapter final : public Scale declares public inheritance: the adapter may be used wherever a Scale is required. This is a type relationship, not a statement that the adapter owns a Scale object. The inherited pure virtual function, marked = 0 in Scale, demands an implementation. The override word asks the compiler to check that grams matches it, including its final const. A misspelled name or missing const produces a compile error instead of a hidden new method. final prevents further derivation; this example does not need another layer of subclasses.

blocks.text: At compilation, the compiler checks that light_enough may call grams through const Scale&. At execution, virtual dispatch selects ScaleAdapter::grams for our actual object. The ampersand makes scale a reference, so the function borrows the existing object rather than copying it. const prevents that call from modifying the object through this interface. It does not prove the physical sensor never changes. Here the simulated device stores one fixed reading, making our printed results repeatable.

ScaleAdapter also contains a reference, device_. Its constructor stores a connection to a LegacyScale that already exists. No device copy is made; no allocation is needed. The caller must keep that device alive for every adapter call. main creates device first and scale second. Local objects are destroyed in reverse order, so the adapter goes away before the device. Destroying the adapter does not destroy the borrowed device. Scale has a virtual destructor so a future owner holding a base-class pointer can destroy a derived adapter correctly.

topics.title: Units and errors are part of the contract
topics.summary: A boundary must translate meanings, not just names. In grams(), raw is checked before conversion. The value -1 is an error marker, not negative physical weight. Throwing std::runtime_error ends the normal call, so light_enough cannot accidentally accept the parcel. The error reaches the test's matching catch block. The adapter leaves both itself and its device unchanged when the call fails.

blocks.text: Dividing two integers discards the fractional part. Writing 1000.0 makes the divisor a double; the integer is converted for floating-point division. The returned double represents grams. This does not make floating-point arithmetic exact for every fraction. The test therefore uses a small tolerance when checking 1.25. The exact boundary values used here, two and zero, are represented exactly. A measurement system with strict legal or scientific rounding rules would need an explicit rule and perhaps an integer base unit throughout.

The contract assumes nonnegative integer milligrams are valid readings and all negatives signal failure. Real devices may distinguish timeout, overload, and calibration errors. An adapter should preserve distinctions the application needs instead of flattening every failure into zero. It should also avoid inventing precision: dividing an integer milligram count does not create a more precise measurement.

topics.title: Composition and multiple inheritance
topics.summary: C++ also permits a class to inherit from two bases. A class adapter could inherit from Scale and LegacyScale, then use the inherited milligrams member. That approach may fit a legacy class designed for derivation, especially when overriding its virtual behavior is necessary. However, the adapter then contains its own legacy base subobject. It cannot automatically wrap the device instance that the application already owns. Public inheritance from the legacy type can also expose operations the new interface was meant to hide.

blocks.text: Our object adapter uses composition in the broad design sense of holding a connection to another object. The connection is borrowing, so the diagram uses a dependency arrow rather than an ownership diamond. It keeps lifetime policy with main and permits several adapters to view one device when that is intended. If the adapter should control the device's lifetime, a value member or unique_ptr would state a different ownership rule. Choose that rule from the actual device lifecycle, not from the pattern's name.

When debugging an adapter, write down three things before changing code: the input unit and error range, the target unit and error contract, and the lifetime owner. A wrong answer can come from any of them. When replacing a device library, keep the parcel tests unchanged and add device-specific adapter tests. That small boundary limits how far vendor changes travel through the program.

topics.summary: A gram-based parcel rule

blocks.title: Requirements
items: Accept an existing LegacyScale without changing its class.
Return fractional grams and reject every negative raw reading.
Accept exactly two grams and reject a heavier sample.

blocks.text: Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.

blocks.title: Invariants
items: The adapter never owns or deletes device_.
A successful grams call returns a nonnegative value in grams.
Device failure never becomes a successful parcel decision.

blocks.text: Alternative: A free conversion function is simpler if all callers can use it. A multiple-inheritance adapter can reuse protected legacy behavior but ties the adapter to a legacy base subobject and its construction rules.

Verification: The executable checks 1250, zero, the 2000 boundary, 2001, and -1. It verifies both the translated value and the client rule. It does not test real hardware timing or every possible device error.
Maintenance: Keep the adapter next to the integration code. Application rules should speak in application units and depend on stable contracts.

workshop.title: A gram-based parcel rule
workshop.problem: A gram-based parcel rule. Accept an existing LegacyScale without changing its class. Return fractional grams and reject every negative raw reading. Accept exactly two grams and reject a heavier sample.

steps.why: main owns the old device and the adapter borrows it.
The reading is accepted as a measurement.
Division changes the unit; 1.25 is at most 2.0.
No negative error marker is returned as grams.

workshop.pitfall: Divide raw by integer 1000. A raw value of 1250 becomes 1 gram instead of 1.25. Integer division discards the remainder before conversion to double.

discussion.question: A one-file script reads one device once, and no caller accepts Scale. Choose a free helper or an adapter class and explain the deciding constraint.
discussion.answer: Use a free helper that validates and converts. No runtime interface needs an adapter object. Choose the class when callers already use Scale or need interchangeable device implementations.
discussion.hint: The object interface exists to satisfy an actual caller.

workshop.alternative: A free conversion function is simpler if all callers can use it. A multiple-inheritance adapter can reuse protected legacy behavior but ties the adapter to a legacy base subobject and its construction rules.
workshop.design: Use one borrowing adapter because the existing rule depends on Scale and the physical device already has an owner. Keep conversion and device-error checks together.
invariants: The adapter never owns or deletes device_.
A successful grams call returns a nonnegative value in grams.
Device failure never becomes a successful parcel decision.
workshop.maintenance: Keep the adapter next to the integration code. Application rules should speak in application units and depend on stable contracts.
workshop.verification: The executable checks 1250, zero, the 2000 boundary, 2001, and -1. It verifies both the translated value and the client rule. It does not test real hardware timing or every possible device error.
